clue.text: Old newspaper worker, sort with The Sun, perhaps?

parts.note: sort and type both mean a kind or class of thing
the sun sets each evening, so it is something that sets

explanation.surface: A veteran printer at a tabloid gets lumped in with the staff of The Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun looks like the tabloid, which suits the newspaper surface, but here it is the thing in the sky that sets; 'perhaps' warns it is only one example of a setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Before computers, compositors arranged metal type by hand to make up each printed page of the paper.

clue.text: Cheers, cheers, cheers!

parts.note: ta is informal British thanks, as is cheers
a second thank-you, the same short word again

explanation.surface: Someone raises a glass three times over in noisy celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech 'cheers' means thanks and also goodbye; ta is casual British thanks, so two of them side by side make the farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ta-ta is a chatty British farewell, and 'cheers' is commonly used to say goodbye when parting.

clue.text: Breathe heavily on that woman's cat

indicators.note: in a down entry, one part sitting on another means the first stands above the second

parts.note: to pant is to breathe hard and fast
her is the possessive for a woman already mentioned

explanation.surface: Someone puffs warm breath over a lady's pet cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s makes 'cat' look owned by the woman, but 'that woman's' simply gives the possessive pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: A panther is a large wild feline, usually a black leopard or jaguar, so it is a big species of cat.

clue.text: Doing nicely in session, quite!

parts.note: a sitting is a session, as of a parliament or court
pretty good means quite good

explanation.surface: Someone praises how well a meeting or lesson is going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite!' reads as an exclamation of agreement, but it is an adverb meaning fairly, the same as pretty in 'pretty good'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sitting pretty is an idiom for being in a comfortable, advantageous position, faring well.

clue.text: Religious education brought in is to me terribly boring

indicators.note: something brought in is taken inside, so it ends up enclosed by other letters
done terribly means done badly, so the letters come out in a muddled order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
RE is the school subject abbreviation

explanation.surface: A pupil complains that scripture lessons are dreadfully dull.
explanation.walkthrough: RE, short for religious education, is a compulsory subject in British schools; it slots between the second and third letters of the rearranged words.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiresome describes something tedious that wears out your patience, which is exactly what boring means.

clue.text: Plaque with top scratched, repaired so just the same

indicators.note: scratching off the top of a down word removes its first letter
something repaired is put back together, with its parts rearranged into working order

parts.note: the word minus its opening P

explanation.surface: A damaged commemorative plaque is restored to look exactly as before.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the top of a word is its first letter; what is left is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Equal means identical in amount or value, so two things that are equal are just the same.

clue.text: Tweeter in prison?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a creature that tweets, a songbird
second meaning: British slang for time in jail

explanation.surface: Someone posting on Twitter from behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweeter suggests a social media user, but it is the feathered kind. 'Doing bird' is British slang for serving a prison sentence, from rhyming slang bird-lime for time.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweeting creature is a songbird, and in British slang the same word means a jail term.

clue.text: First contained by that, I and almost everyone

indicators.note: almost all of something is short of the whole, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: what is contained is in something
it and that both point at a thing
taken as written
all means every person

explanation.surface: A puzzling list of pronouns, seemingly about what is first held inside what.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contained by' looks like a container instruction, but here it simply supplies the little word for being inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Initial is an adjective for what comes at the beginning, so it can replace first in a sentence.

clue.text: Rude drunk ready to go, last of lager guzzled

indicators.note: what is guzzled is swallowed whole, so it ends up inside
someone drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the last of a word is its closing letter alone

parts.note: the final letter of the beer

explanation.surface: A boorish drinker is set to leave once the beer has been downed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like it describes the rude person, but it is the signal to scramble the three words once the extra letter is swallowed among them.
explanation.definitionFit: Derogatory remarks are disparaging and disrespectful, which is what rude means of speech.

clue.text: Rule, last of three in camp?

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a tent is a camp's shelter; the question mark flags this loose example

indicators.note: the last of a word is only its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the number

explanation.surface: A campsite rule that the third arrival must sleep elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a tent is only a stand-in for a camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or doctrine held as true, and a rule can mean such a guiding principle.

clue.text: Dirtier Hurricane flying all over the place

indicators.note: things flying all over the place are scattered, so the letters land in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A storm, or a Hurricane fighter plane, whips grime everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital H suggests the wartime fighter plane, but the word is just a set of letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Raunchy means coarse or sexually explicit, and dirty is a common word for crude or smutty content.

clue.text: Measure up and take scissors to salad leaves?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an idiom for meeting the required standard
second meaning, taken literally: snipping the seedling crop grown with cress

explanation.walkthrough: Mustard and cress is a classic British sandwich garnish of seedlings snipped with scissors, which makes the idiom literal.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut the mustard is to be good enough, an idiom for meeting expectations; literally it is trimming seedling greens.

clue.text: Shock describing intense headache, finding fault easily

definitions.note: adjective phrase, matching hair-splitting used as an adjective

parts.note: a shock of hair is a thick mass of it
a very bad headache is called a splitting one

explanation.surface: A jolt that brings on a migraine leaves someone quick to complain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' suggests a fright, but here it is a thick mop of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair-splitting describes quibbling over tiny distinctions, so someone hair-splitting is quick to find trivial faults.

clue.text: Cable in one car adapted for ship

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed within it
something adapted is altered and reworked, so its letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a cable is a line, as for telephones

explanation.surface: A motorist's single vehicle has its wiring modified to suit a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged words are split open, with the cable word placed before their last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocean liner is a large passenger vessel built for long sea crossings, so it is a kind of ship.

clue.text: Amusing person, willing cheat, for example

parts.note: a card is an old word for a joker or wag
game for anything means willing

explanation.surface: A comedian who is happy to bend the rules is described as a cheat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheat' reads as a person, but it is the name of a game in which players lie about the cards they lay down.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheat, also called I Doubt It, is a game played with a pack of playing cards, so it is one example.

clue.text: Holiday home offering tea leased out

parts.note: cha is British slang for tea
a let property is one rented to tenants

explanation.surface: A rented holiday cottage comes with a welcome cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Cha, from the Chinese, is old British slang for a cup of tea; 'offering' only joins the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a wooden cabin, often at a ski resort or camp, used for vacation stays.

clue.text: Anchor in sea for example securing boat finally

parts.note: the main is a poetic word for the open sea

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece grips another inside it

parts.note: say introduces an example, as for example does

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of a word, its closing letter

parts.note: the closing letter of the vessel

explanation.surface: Mooring a vessel by dropping its anchor into the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anchor' looks nautical alongside sea and boat, but it means a person or thing everything relies on.
explanation.definitionFit: A mainstay is the chief support on which something depends, the figurative sense of anchor.

clue.text: Agree a company should be led by leader in fact!

indicators.note: being led by something means having it go in front

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
a firm is a business company

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a business ought to be run on hard facts.
explanation.walkthrough: The single A stands first; the business word is led by the letter that heads the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: To affirm is to state that something is true or give assent, a synonym for agree.

clue.text: European country without the right to gather in funds

indicators.note: to gather something is to draw it in close, so it ends up inside
without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: the country west of Germany
R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A European nation without the legal right to raise money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In funds' looks like a phrase meaning having money, but in is the piece to be gathered and funds alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Finance can mean money resources available to a business or government, a synonym of funds.

clue.text: Measurer of fuel in gallons steamer used

parts.note: g is the abbreviation for gallons

indicators.note: something used is worn and altered from its original state, so the letters change order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Gauging how many gallons of fuel a steamship has burned.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'in gallons' sound like the unit of measurement, but in only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas meter records how much gas a household consumes, and gas is a domestic fuel.

clue.text: Beyond river is exciting drive, say

indicators.note: what lies beyond something comes after it, so one part follows the other

parts.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England
hot can mean thrilling or exciting, as in a hot ticket

explanation.surface: A thrilling car journey out past the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' suggests motoring, but in golf a drive is a long shot from the tee; 'say' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's opening stroke on each hole is played from the tee, and a drive is the usual example.

clue.text: Greeting neologism, teen discombobulated

indicators.note: discombobulated means confused and thrown into disorder, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bewildered teenager hears a newly coined word of welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neologism' looks like part of the definition, since the phrase is itself a quirky coinage, but every letter of it goes into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase is a jocular hello to someone you have not met for a while, so it is a salutation.

clue.text: Polynesian people residing in Panama or Indonesia

indicators.note: something residing in a place lives within it, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: runs from the end of the first word through the start of the third

explanation.surface: Pacific islanders living in Central America or South-East Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a geography question about where these islanders live, but the place names only house the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The indigenous people of New Zealand are of Polynesian descent, settling there from eastern Polynesia.

clue.text: Mark seems confident about result, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A teacher's grade on a paper shows assurance about the outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a name or a school grade, but it is the definition, a blemish on skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the lasting trace a healed wound leaves on skin, a kind of mark.

clue.text: Childminder, best ever mother of kids

parts.note: a nanny looks after children
GOAT is the acronym for greatest of all time

explanation.surface: Praise for a babysitter as the best there has ever been, a true mother to the children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kids' looks like human children, in keeping with the childminder, but they are young goats.
explanation.definitionFit: Young goats are called kids, and the female adult goat that bears them is a nanny.

clue.text: Bill needs endless wine for a particular purpose

indicators.note: without an end, a word loses its final letter

parts.note: a bill is a poster or advertisement, shortened to ad
hock is a British name for German white wine

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill needs a bottle that never runs out, for some specific reason.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name or an invoice, but it is a posted notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad hoc is Latin for 'to this', describing something arranged solely for one specific need.

clue.text: 6 Across back, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: going by how something sounds means the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: the rear is the back; in a non-rhotic British accent the two are said alike

explanation.surface: Asking whether the bird's hindquarters sound like something.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 Across is BIRD, so the definition is a bird; the homophone relies on the British pronunciation that drops the final r.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhea is a large flightless South American ratite, related to the ostrich, so it is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Heartless trite idiocy excited journalist

indicators.note: without a heart, a word loses its central letter
excited means stirred up, so the letters are agitated into a new order

parts.note: the word minus its middle letter I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A reporter gets worked up over cruel, banal stupidity.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the City editor runs a paper's financial news, named after the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A city editor is a senior newspaper journalist in charge of business coverage or local news.
